h: חַג הַפֶּסַח, מַאֲמָר ל׳ Pesach — Maamar Lamed

p: sought out by all who desire them"
that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world
is so that man should take from it
a lesson for the service of Hashem,
and that He created everything for His glory.
And as they said in the name of
רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ מִפְּשִׁיסְחָא זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה,
our holy Rebbe of Peshischa, of blessed memory,
that His name is called Shakai
because He said to His world "Enough" (dai) —
to learn from it recognition of Hashem, may He be blessed.
And when Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, came
"Is it possible for a palace to be without a master?"
עַד שֶׁהֵצִיץ עָלָיו הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
until the Holy One, blessed be He, looked out upon him
and said to him, "I am the master of the palace"
And with this he explained what is said
"The earth is full of Your possessions (kinyanecha)" —
that is, the whole earth is filled with acquisitions
through which a person may acquire
knowledge of Hashem, may He be blessed,
and what Hashem, may He be blessed, wants of him.
וְכָל דָּבָר שֶׁבָּא לְנֶגֶד עֵינֵי הָאָדָם,
And everything that comes before a person's eyes,
by intent and by individual providence
did this thing chance before his eyes,
so that he should teach himself from it.
מֵרַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ רַבִּי ר' זוּשָׁא זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה,
of our holy Rebbe, Reb Zusha, of blessed memory,
that he was walking innocently along the road,
and a gentile came toward him
and asked him to help him
(which they call "hay," like the letter Hei)
And he told him that he could not,
"You can, but you do not want to."
וְאָמַר עַל זֶה רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
And our aforementioned holy Rebbe said about this
that they were hinting to him
that the lower Hei had fallen,
and it was within his ability to raise it up,
only he did not want to.
"Why is the portion of the nazir juxtaposed
to the portion of the sotah?
that whoever sees a sotah in her disgrace
Rather it is as we said:
since Hashem, may He be blessed, arranged
before his eyes the sotah in her disgrace,
And this is what is said:
in that they are "sought out by all who desire them,"
some lesson for His service, blessed be His name,
can take it for himself from the works of Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 12a — "Reish Lakish said: What is meant by 'I am E-l Shaddai'? I am the One who said to the world 'Enough (dai)!'" — when the world, as it was being created, kept expanding until the Holy One rebuked it and made it stand. (Rashi has no comment on this line.)

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 39:1 — "A parable: one passing from place to place saw a palace aflame. He said: 'Could this palace be without a master?' The owner peered out and said: 'I am the master of the palace.' So, because Avraham said, 'Could this world be without a guide?' the Holy One peered out and said: 'I am the Master of the world.'"

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Dov Ber of Mezritch, Maggid Devarav LeYaakov 16 — “‘Or he saw’: he sees the deeds of another and is reminded of his own deeds. For whatever a person sees, he should take to heart: why did the Holy One, blessed is He, show me this? Is not everything by individual providence? Rather, if he sees a sinful thing, he should think: presumably I too have done some trace of it, even if I did not do exactly this. And this is ‘or he saw’: he sees a sin in another person, and it reminds him of something he himself has done.” Connection: The Maggid likewise holds that whatever comes before a person's eyes is shown him by individual providence as a lesson; he adds that a sin one witnesses points to a trace of the same failing in oneself, the logic behind the nazir learning from the sotah.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 2a — "Rebbi says: Why is the section of the Nazir placed next to the section of the Sotah? To tell you that whoever sees a sotah in her degradation should abstain from wine." Rashi: in her degradation — disgraced and made repulsive, as the Mishnah describes.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Naso 13 — “Whatever happens before a person by chance is a hint from Above, so that he may take from them a hint of wisdom… So in the Written Torah the sotah is mentioned before the nazir: from his chancing to see this he must understand that surely he must separate himself from wine. But in the Oral Torah, in the Gemara, Nazir is placed before Sotah. This is ‘one who sees what will be born’: out of his wisdom he sees beforehand what could come of a thing before it happens to him, and separates himself from wine.” Connection: It reads the Sotah–Nazir juxtaposition, with the same story of Reb Zusha, as here, and adds that the Oral Torah reverses the order for the wise man who sees the outcome before it is shown to him.
